regions.label: The wings
regions.text: Behind the painted flats wait the others: the shadowed legs of the corps de ballet under drooping skirts, and a man in black evening dress, faceless, hands in his pockets. He is an abonné — a season subscriber of the Paris Opéra, one of the men whose subscription bought the run of the wings and whose favour could make a dancer's career. Degas states the fact without comment, in the corner, where such facts actually stood.

regions.label: The star
regions.text: She is caught at the instant of the révérence, the bow taken alone after a solo: chin lifted, throat bare, eyes closed, one shoulder dipped. The footlights strike her from below — the lighting that makes theatrical faces strange — and burn the front of her tutu to a white flare scattered with flower colour. The sheet is pastel worked over a printed monotype, which is what gives the light its powdery, granular flare.

regions.label: The stage floor
regions.text: We look down from a box above the stage, so the floor tips up behind the dancer like a wall of amber light and she floats against it with nothing else in focus. The viewpoint is the picture's first invention and its most modern feature — an angle no earlier painter of the theatre would have chosen, borrowed from the sightlines of the building itself and from the cropped framing of photography.
